chapter.title: Derivatives of Derivatives: Going Higher
chapter.summary: Nothing stops a derivative from being differentiated again; repeating the process builds a hierarchy of higher order derivatives, each one measuring how the previous rate of change is itself changing.
chapter.body:
The derivative f'(x) is itself a function of x, built from f using the limit definition or the differentiation rules developed so far. Since f' is a function just like f was, there is nothing stopping it from being differentiated again. The result, f''(x), is called the second derivative. Differentiating once more gives the third derivative f'''(x), and the process can continue indefinitely, as long as each new function remains differentiable.

Prime notation gets unwieldy after two or three marks, so beyond that point the standard notation switches to f^(n)(x), read as f to the n, with f^(0)(x) simply meaning the original function. In Leibniz notation the pattern is d^n y/dx^n, formed by stacking the differentiation operator d/dx on itself n times: d^2y/dx^2 for the second derivative, d^3y/dx^3 for the third, and so on.

As a worked example, take the polynomial f(x) = x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x. Then f'(x) = 4x^3 - 9x^2 + 2, f''(x) = 12x^2 - 18x, f'''(x) = 24x - 18, f''''(x) = 24, and f^(5)(x) = 0, with every derivative after that also equal to 0. In general, a degree n polynomial has exactly n nonzero derivatives before the derivatives permanently hit zero, a handy check when verifying work by hand.

Contrast that with a function whose derivatives never terminate: f(x) = sin x. Then f'(x) = cos x, f''(x) = -sin x, f'''(x) = -cos x, f''''(x) = sin x, and the pattern repeats exactly from there, cycling with period four forever. This kind of cyclical behavior under repeated differentiation shows up constantly later on, especially when describing oscillating systems.

The second derivative in particular carries two vivid meanings, one physical and one graphical, concavity, which together make it worth a dedicated look in the next chapter.

chapter.title: Why Numbers Need a Story: An Introduction to Statistics
chapter.summary: This section introduces statistics as the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data to answer questions and make decisions in the presence of uncertainty.
chapter.body:
Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data in order to answer questions and make decisions when the world is uncertain. Notice that word: uncertain. If every measurement came out exactly the same every time, we would not need statistics at all. We would just measure something once and know the truth forever. But real measurements vary. Two students who each shoot ten free throws will not make the same number of shots. Two batches of the same cookie recipe will not weigh exactly the same. Statistics exists because variability is a basic fact of the world, and we need reliable tools for describing it, learning from it, and making decisions in spite of it.

It helps to think of statistics as a four step process. First, you collect data by observing, measuring, or surveying. Second, you organize and summarize that data so a huge pile of numbers becomes something a human being can actually look at, such as a table, a graph, or a single summary number like an average. Third, you analyze the data, looking for patterns, comparing groups, or checking whether a pattern is more than just random noise. Fourth, you interpret the results in plain language and connect them back to the original question. Skipping any one of these steps is how people end up misusing data, either by collecting it carelessly or by drawing conclusions the data cannot actually support.

Statistics is traditionally split into two branches. Descriptive statistics is about summarizing and displaying the data you actually have in hand, using tools like averages, percentages, and charts. Inferential statistics goes a step further: it uses data from a smaller group to draw conclusions about a much larger group that was not fully measured. Both branches depend on the same underlying data, but they answer different kinds of questions. Descriptive statistics answers "what did we observe." Inferential statistics answers "what can we conclude beyond what we observed."

Here is a small worked example of descriptive statistics in action. Suppose a basketball player attempts 10 free throws in practice and makes 7 of them. The proportion made is calculated by dividing the number of successes by the number of attempts: 7 divided by 10 equals 0.70, or 70 percent. That single number, 70 percent, is a statistic, a number that summarizes something about the data. It is useful, but it also has limits. Ten shots is a small number of attempts, so if the player shot another 10 free throws the next day, the result might be 6 makes, or 9 makes, purely due to chance. A large part of learning statistics is learning how much to trust a number like 70 percent, and how that trust changes as the amount of data grows.

Every other idea in this course builds on this foundation. Before you can summarize or analyze anything, you need data to work with, which is the subject of the next section. From there, you will learn how to describe individual pieces of information as variables and observations, how to organize them into datasets, and eventually how to use a manageable sample to learn something true about an entire population. Statistics, in other words, is the toolbox. The rest of this course is about learning to use each tool correctly.

chapter.title: Let the Units Do the Work: Dimensional Analysis
chapter.summary: Dimensional analysis uses unit conversion factors, built from SI base units, as a self checking method for turning one quantity into another without guessing whether to multiply or divide.
chapter.body:
Dimensional analysis, also called the factor label method, is a problem solving strategy that treats units as algebraic quantities you can multiply, divide, and cancel just like numbers. It builds directly on SI Units, since chemistry relies on a small set of base units, meters for length, kilograms for mass, seconds for time, moles for amount of substance, and derived units built from them, and on Significant Figures, since a converted answer must still respect the precision of the original measurement. The core idea is simple: any quantity can be multiplied by a conversion factor, a fraction equal to 1 because its numerator and denominator represent the same physical amount, without changing the actual quantity, only the units it is expressed in.

A conversion factor comes from an equality between two units, such as 1 inch equals 2.54 centimeters, or 1000 milliliters equals 1 liter. Because both sides of that equality describe the same physical amount, the fraction 2.54 cm over 1 in, or its flip, 1 in over 2.54 cm, is equal to 1, and multiplying any quantity by 1 never changes its true value. The skill lies in choosing which version of the fraction to use, and dimensional analysis makes that choice almost automatic: you set up the fraction so the unit you want to cancel sits opposite where it appears in your starting quantity, leaving only the unit you want in the final answer.

Consider converting 3.5 kilometers to centimeters, a two step conversion. Starting with 3.5 km, multiply by the conversion factor 1000 m over 1 km, which cancels the km, leaving meters: 3.5 km x (1000 m / 1 km) = 3500 m. Then multiply by 100 cm over 1 m, which cancels the m, leaving centimeters: 3500 m x (100 cm / 1 m) = 350000 cm, or 3.5 x 10^5 cm in scientific notation. Notice that at every step, the unit being eliminated appears once in the numerator of the running quantity and once in the denominator of the conversion factor, so it cancels cleanly, and the only units left standing at the end are the ones you were asked for.

Chemistry problems often chain several conversion factors in a single setup, moving from one kind of unit to a completely different kind, such as converting a volume of gas into a number of molecules, or a mass of reactant into moles of product. The method works exactly the same way no matter how many factors are strung together: write the given quantity, then multiply by one conversion factor after another, canceling units as you go, until only the desired unit remains uncancelled. For example, finding how many seconds are in exactly 2.0 days uses two factors: 2.0 days x (24 h / 1 day) x (3600 s / 1 h) = 172800 s, which rounds to 1.7 x 10^5 s given that 2.0 days has two significant figures.

The real value of dimensional analysis is that it catches mistakes before you even finish the arithmetic. If you accidentally set up a conversion factor upside down, the units will not cancel properly, and you will be left with a nonsensical combination like cm times km instead of a clean single unit, which is an immediate signal that something in the setup is wrong. That built in error check is why this method remains the standard approach across chemistry, physics, and engineering for any problem that involves converting between units or combining several measured quantities into one final result.

PROBLEMS.forEach(problem => {
  if (!problem.targetValue) {
    let val = problem.startValue;
    problem.factorIds.forEach(id => {
      const f = FACTORS[id];
      val *= f.numeratorValue / f.denominatorValue;
    });
    problem.targetValue = val;
  }

function setup() {
  parentEl = document.querySelector('main');
  updateCanvasSize();
  const canvas = createCanvas(canvasWidth, canvasHeight);
  canvas.parent(parentEl);

  newProblemBtn = createButton('New Problem');
  newProblemBtn.mousePressed(() => startNewProblem());

  checkBtn = createButton('Check Answer');
  checkBtn.mousePressed(() => checkAnswer());

  undoBtn = createButton('Undo Last Factor');
  undoBtn.mousePressed(() => {
    workspaceChain.pop();
    statusMessage = 'Removed the most recent conversion factor.';
  });

  positionControls();
  startNewProblem();
}

function positionControls() {
  const y = drawHeight + 12;
  if (newProblemBtn) newProblemBtn.position(margin, y);
  if (checkBtn) checkBtn.position(margin + 160, y);
  if (undoBtn) undoBtn.position(margin + 320, y);
}

function updateCanvasSize() {
  const containerWidth = parentEl ? parentEl.clientWidth : 0;
  const fallbackWidth = window.innerWidth || windowWidth || 960;
  const targetWidth = containerWidth > 0 ? containerWidth : fallbackWidth;
  if (Math.abs(targetWidth - canvasWidth) > 2) {
    canvasWidth = targetWidth;
    resizeCanvas?.(canvasWidth, canvasHeight);
    positionControls();
  }
}

function windowResized() {
  updateCanvasSize();
}

function startNewProblem() {
  currentProblem = random(PROBLEMS);
  workspaceChain = [];
  statusMessage = 'Click a conversion tile to add it to the workspace.';
  buildFactorSet();
}

function buildFactorSet() {
  const ids = [...currentProblem.factorIds];
  const distractors = [...(currentProblem.distractors || [])];
  shuffleArray(distractors);
  while (ids.length < Math.min(6, currentProblem.factorIds.length + distractors.length)) {
    const next = distractors.shift();
    if (!next) break;
    if (!ids.includes(next)) ids.push(next);
  }
  shuffleArray(ids);
  availableFactorIds = ids;
}

function draw() {
  updateCanvasSize();

  // Drawing area background
  noStroke();
  fill('aliceblue');
  rect(0, 0, canvasWidth, drawHeight);

  // Control strip background
  fill('white');
  rect(0, drawHeight, canvasWidth, controlHeight);
  stroke('#c7d7ef');
  line(0, drawHeight, canvasWidth, drawHeight);
  noStroke();

  if (!currentProblem) return;

  drawHeader();
  drawWorkspace();
  drawUnitPanel();
  drawFactorTray();
  drawCelebration();
  drawControlStrip();
}

function drawHeader() {
  fill('#073b4c');
  textSize(24);
  textStyle(BOLD);
  text('Dimensional Analysis Practice', margin, 32);

  textSize(16);
  textStyle(NORMAL);
  text(`Level ${currentProblem.level} • ${currentProblem.prompt}`, margin, 60);

  fill('#073b4c');
  const scoreText = scoreAttempts > 0 ? `${scoreCorrect}/${scoreAttempts} correct` : '0 problems attempted';
  textAlign(RIGHT, TOP);
  text(`Score: ${scoreText}`, canvasWidth - margin, 20);
  textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);
}

function drawWorkspace() {
  const y = 190;
  fill('#ffffff');
  stroke('#d1e8e2');
  const workspaceHeight = workspaceCardHeight * 1.6;
  rect(margin - 8, y - workspaceCardHeight, canvasWidth - margin * 2 + 16, workspaceHeight, 12);
  noStroke();

  let currentLeft = margin;
  const startLabel = `${currentProblem.startValue.toFixed(3)} ${currentProblem.startUnitLabel}`;
  drawValueCard(currentLeft, y, startLabel);
  let lastRight = currentLeft + workspaceCardWidth;

  workspaceChain.forEach(factor => {
    fill('#073b4c');
    textSize(24);
    textAlign(CENTER, CENTER);
    text('×', lastRight + workspaceCardSpacing / 2, y);
    textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);
    currentLeft = lastRight + workspaceCardSpacing;
    drawFractionCard(currentLeft, y, factor);
    lastRight = currentLeft + workspaceCardWidth;
  });

  fill('#073b4c');
  textSize(24);
  textAlign(CENTER, CENTER);
  text('=', lastRight + workspaceCardSpacing / 2, y);
  textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);

  const evaluation = evaluateChain();
  const finalUnits = formatUnits(evaluation.numCounts, evaluation.denCounts);
  const valueText = `${formatValue(evaluation.value)} ${finalUnits}`;
  drawValueCard(lastRight + workspaceCardSpacing, y, valueText, '#ffd166');

  fill('#0b3954');
  textSize(16);
  text(statusMessage, margin, y + workspaceCardHeight);
}

function drawValueCard(x, y, textValue, fillColor = '#118ab2') {
  fill(fillColor);
  noStroke();
  rect(x, y - workspaceCardHeight / 2, workspaceCardWidth, workspaceCardHeight, 14);
  fill('#ffffff');
  textSize(16);
  textAlign(CENTER, CENTER);
  text(textValue, x + workspaceCardWidth / 2, y);
  textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);
}

function drawFractionCard(x, y, factor) {
  fill('#ffffff');
  stroke(factor.color);
  strokeWeight(2);
  rect(x, y - workspaceCardHeight / 2, workspaceCardWidth, workspaceCardHeight, 14);
  noStroke();
  fill('#073b4c');
  textSize(15);
  textAlign(CENTER, CENTER);
  text(`${factor.numeratorValue} ${factor.numeratorUnits.join('·')}`, x + workspaceCardWidth / 2, y - 14);
  text(`${factor.denominatorValue} ${factor.denominatorUnits.join('·')}`, x + workspaceCardWidth / 2, y + 14);
  textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);
}

function drawUnitPanel() {
  const result = evaluateChain();
  const panelY = 290;
  const panelH = 90;
  fill('#f0f4ff');
  noStroke();
  rect(margin - 10, panelY, canvasWidth - margin * 2 + 20, panelH, 12);

  fill('#073b4c');
  textSize(16);
  text('Unit cancellation tracker', margin, panelY + 24);

  textSize(14);
  drawUnitColumn(margin, panelY + 50, 'Numerator', result.rawNumerator, result.numCounts);
  drawUnitColumn(canvasWidth / 2, panelY + 50, 'Denominator', result.rawDenominator, result.denCounts);
}

function drawUnitColumn(x, y, label, rawCounts, remainingCounts) {
  fill('#118ab2');
  text(label, x, y);
  let offset = 18;
  Object.keys(rawCounts).forEach(unit => {
    const raw = rawCounts[unit] || 0;
    const remaining = remainingCounts[unit] || 0;
    if (raw === 0) return;
    const textY = y + offset;
    if (remaining === 0) {
      fill('#118a0a');
      text(`${unit} canceled`, x, textY);
      stroke('#118a0a');
      line(x, textY - 6, x + textWidth(`${unit} canceled`), textY - 6);
      noStroke();
    } else {
      fill('#ef476f');
      textStyle(BOLD);
      text(`${unit} × ${remaining}`, x, textY);
      textStyle(NORMAL);
    }
    offset += 20;
  });
}

function drawFactorTray() {
  const trayHeight = 190;
  const trayY = drawHeight - trayHeight - 12;
  fill('#083d77');
  rect(0, trayY, canvasWidth, trayHeight);
  fill('#f7fff7');
  textSize(16);
  textAlign(CENTER, TOP);
  text('Conversion factor tiles (click to add to the workspace):', canvasWidth / 2, trayY + 14);

  const columns = max(3, floor(canvasWidth / 220));
  const totalPadding = 40;
  const available = canvasWidth - totalPadding;
  const spacing = 12;
  const cardWidth = (available - (columns - 1) * spacing) / columns;
  const cardHeight = 58;
  factorCardLayout = [];

  availableFactorIds.forEach((id, idx) => {
    const factor = FACTORS[id];
    const row = floor(idx / columns);
    const col = idx % columns;
    const startX = (canvasWidth - (cardWidth * columns + spacing * (columns - 1))) / 2;
    const x = startX + col * (cardWidth + spacing);
    const y = trayY + 44 + row * (cardHeight + 12);

    const hovered = mouseX >= x && mouseX <= x + cardWidth && mouseY >= y && mouseY <= y + cardHeight;
    fill(hovered ? '#ffe066' : '#ffffff');
    stroke(factor.color);
    strokeWeight(2);
    rect(x, y, cardWidth, cardHeight, 10);
    noStroke();
    fill('#073b4c');
    textAlign(CENTER, CENTER);
    textSize(14);
    text(factor.label, x + cardWidth / 2, y + cardHeight / 2);
    textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);

    factorCardLayout.push({ id, x, y, w: cardWidth, h: cardHeight });
  });
}

function drawControlStrip() {
  fill('#0f172a');
  textSize(15);
  textAlign(LEFT, CENTER);
  const message = 'Click tiles to build the conversion chain, then press Check Answer. Undo removes the last tile.';
  text(message, margin, drawHeight + controlHeight / 2);
  textAlign(LEFT, BASELINE);
}

function mousePressed() {
  for (const card of factorCardLayout) {
    if (mouseX >= card.x && mouseX <= card.x + card.w && mouseY >= card.y && mouseY <= card.y + card.h) {
      workspaceChain.push(FACTORS[card.id]);
      statusMessage = `Added ${FACTORS[card.id].label}`;
      return;
    }
  }
}

function evaluateChain() {
  if (!currentProblem) {
    return {
      value: 0,
      numCounts: {},
      denCounts: {},
      rawNumerator: {},
      rawDenominator: {}
    };
  }
  let value = currentProblem.startValue;
  const rawNumerator = {};
  const rawDenominator = {};
  const numCounts = {};
  const denCounts = {};

  const addUnits = (counts, units) => {
    units.forEach(unit => {
      counts[unit] = (counts[unit] || 0) + 1;
    });
  };

  addUnits(rawNumerator, currentProblem.startUnits.num);
  addUnits(numCounts, currentProblem.startUnits.num);
  addUnits(rawDenominator, currentProblem.startUnits.den);
  addUnits(denCounts, currentProblem.startUnits.den);

  workspaceChain.forEach(factor => {
    value *= factor.numeratorValue / factor.denominatorValue;
    addUnits(rawNumerator, factor.numeratorUnits);
    addUnits(numCounts, factor.numeratorUnits);
    addUnits(rawDenominator, factor.denominatorUnits);
    addUnits(denCounts, factor.denominatorUnits);
  });

  const allUnits = new Set([...Object.keys(numCounts), ...Object.keys(denCounts)]);
  allUnits.forEach(unit => {
    const common = Math.min(numCounts[unit] || 0, denCounts[unit] || 0);
    if (common > 0) {
      numCounts[unit] -= common;
      denCounts[unit] -= common;
    }
  });

  return { value, numCounts, denCounts, rawNumerator, rawDenominator };
}

function checkAnswer() {
  if (!currentProblem) return;
  const result = evaluateChain();
  if (workspaceChain.length === 0) {
    statusMessage = 'Add at least one conversion factor before checking.';
    return;
  }
  scoreAttempts += 1;

  const unitsOK = unitsMatchTarget(result);
  const valueOK = valueMatches(result.value, currentProblem.targetValue);

  if (unitsOK && valueOK) {
    scoreCorrect += 1;
    statusMessage = 'Great job! Units cancel and the numeric value matches the target.';
    triggerCelebration();
    startNewProblem();
  } else if (!unitsOK) {
    statusMessage = 'Units do not match the target yet. Revisit your factors.';
  } else {
    statusMessage = `Numeric value off target. Current: ${formatValue(result.value)} ${formatUnits(result.numCounts, result.denCounts)}`;
  }
}

function unitsMatchTarget(result) {
  const compare = (counts, targetList) => {
    const targetCounts = {};
    targetList.forEach(unit => {
      targetCounts[unit] = (targetCounts[unit] || 0) + 1;
    });
    const keys = new Set([...Object.keys(counts), ...Object.keys(targetCounts)]);
    for (const key of keys) {
      if ((counts[key] || 0) !== (targetCounts[key] || 0)) {
        return false;
      }
    }
    return true;
  };
  return compare(result.numCounts, currentProblem.targetUnits.num) && compare(result.denCounts, currentProblem.targetUnits.den);
}

function valueMatches(value, target) {
  if (!isFinite(value)) return false;
  const tolerance = Math.max(0.01, Math.abs(target) * 0.01);
  return Math.abs(value - target) <= tolerance;
}

function formatUnits(numCounts, denCounts) {
  const top = Object.keys(numCounts)
    .filter(key => numCounts[key] > 0)
    .map(key => (numCounts[key] > 1 ? `${key}^${numCounts[key]}` : key));
  const bottom = Object.keys(denCounts)
    .filter(key => denCounts[key] > 0)
    .map(key => (denCounts[key] > 1 ? `${key}^${denCounts[key]}` : key));
  if (top.length === 0 && bottom.length === 0) return '';
  if (bottom.length === 0) return top.join('·');
  if (top.length === 0) return `1/${bottom.join('·')}`;
  return `${top.join('·')}/${bottom.join('·')}`;
}

function formatValue(val) {
  if (Math.abs(val) >= 1000 || Math.abs(val) <= 0.01) {
    return val.toExponential(2);
  }
  return val.toFixed(3);
}

function shuffleArray(arr) {
  for (let i = arr.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
    const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1));
    [arr[i], arr[j]] = [arr[j], arr[i]];
  }
}

function triggerCelebration() {
  celebrationParticles = [];
  const count = 90;
  for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    celebrationParticles.push({
      x: canvasWidth / 2,
      y: drawHeight / 2,
      vx: random(-4.5, 4.5),
      vy: random(-6, -1.5),
      size: random(8, 18),
      life: 120,
      color: color(random(200, 255), random(120, 220), random(120, 255))
    });
  }
}

function drawCelebration() {
  for (let i = celebrationParticles.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
    const p = celebrationParticles[i];
    p.x += p.vx;
    p.y += p.vy;
    p.vy += 0.05;
    p.life -= 1;
    push();
    translate(p.x, p.y);
    fill(p.color);
    noStroke();
    drawStar(p.size);
    pop();
    if (p.life <= 0) celebrationParticles.splice(i, 1);
  }
}

function drawStar(size) {
  beginShape();
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    const angle = i * TWO_PI / 5 - HALF_PI;
    const x = cos(angle) * size;
    const y = sin(angle) * size;
    vertex(x, y);
    const innerAngle = angle + TWO_PI / 10;
    const innerX = cos(innerAngle) * (size / 2);
    const innerY = sin(innerAngle) * (size / 2);
    vertex(innerX, innerY);
  }
  endShape(CLOSE);
}
</script>

chapter.title: Exam Day: Turning a Year of Statistics Into Points
chapter.summary: Converts the course's inference and design skills into concrete tactics for AP Statistics exam pacing, free-response scoring, and avoiding the errors that cost points even when the underlying statistics is correct.
chapter.body:
By this point the statistics itself is done. This last piece is about translating what you know into points under real exam constraints, limited time, a rubric that graders apply mechanically, and a set of habits that cost credit for reasons that have nothing to do with whether you actually understand the material.

On the multiple choice section, know your pacing going in and hold to it, skip and flag a genuinely uncertain question rather than stalling on it. Read stems carefully for negative phrasing, such as which of the following is not true. Pay particular attention to questions that test the scope of inference distinction between random sampling and random assignment, and the bias versus sample size distinction, both covered in this closing unit, since design-reasoning questions like these show up disproportionately and are frequently missed by students who otherwise handle the computational questions well.

On the free-response section, use the four-step process as the literal outline of your answer for any inference question, State, Plan, Do, Conclude, written as separate, clearly labeled parts, because graders award points section by section rather than for a single correct final number. Naming the procedure explicitly, for instance a two-sample t-test for a difference in means, and explicitly listing each condition with a justification tied to the specific numbers in the problem, rather than a bare conditions are met, are both worth dedicated credit, and skipping either one loses points even when the arithmetic that follows is flawless.

Guard specifically against the errors that recur most often: stating the parameter or hypotheses only in symbols with no sentence of context, asserting a condition is met instead of checking it against the problem's actual numbers, interpreting a p-value or confidence interval loosely instead of with the exact template language, treating a fail to reject conclusion as accept H0 or as proof of no difference, and, on design or investigative-task questions, blurring together what a larger sample size fixes, precision and power, with what only a better design fixes, bias and generalizability, the exact distinction this closing unit was built to drill.

The investigative task, usually the final free-response question, often reaches back across the whole course at once: a probability rule from an early unit, a sampling distribution idea, an unfamiliar procedure that has to be reasoned out from first principles rather than recognized and pattern-matched. The same four-step instinct still applies, State what is being asked, Plan an approach even if it is not a named procedure you memorized, Do the work carefully, Conclude in context, but it typically requires drawing on chance and probability rules, design principles from sampling and experiments, and inference logic together in a single question. That is exactly why the course built each unit to be reusable rather than disposable.

None of these tactics substitute for genuine understanding, they only make sure genuine understanding actually converts into a score on exam day. The deeper payoff outlasts the exam itself: reading a claim in the news, a company's write-up of an A or B test, or a public health report, and being able to tell whether the sample size, the study design, and the stated conclusion actually support what is being claimed, is the skill this entire course was built to leave you with.
